title: AFTER — Draft Capstone Presentation: You Would Have Said That

body:
Coming out of the presentation I still would have probably said the project was about AI if somebody asked me quickly, but even then that was not really accurate. I was thinking about how much people rely on AI while at the same time there is this constant fear around it, and I did not want to make another project that just says AI is replacing everyone so be afraid. That did not interest me because I use technology, I like technology and most of the things I make already use technology to reach something bigger than the technology itself.

What felt more interesting was why it becomes useful enough that we willingly give things to it.

At this point I still thought authorship was much stricter than I do now. I was closer to thinking if the human did not completely make it then it is not really theirs. Completely human equals authored, AI involvement starts taking something away. I do not think I would have worded it that clearly at the time, but looking back that was basically the position.

The weird thing is the presentation itself already had cracks in that position because I had literally written a machine that helps first. If help automatically destroys authorship then there is no question. If every tool removes authorship then the project answers itself before it starts. So there was already a contradiction sitting in what I presented and I had not really dealt with it yet.

Another thing I realised was how much I had written without actually testing any of it. I had acts, stages, agency, memory, lying, language, art, movement, interpretation, efficiency, passion and physical interaction. I could explain why every one of them mattered, but I could not yet point at one interaction and say this is the moment where the question actually happens.

That is probably one of the habits I need to watch in this project. I am ambitious with it because the topic lets me go almost anywhere and I genuinely like a lot of those directions. But naming every possible direction does not automatically make the work deeper. It can actually hide the fact that I have not chosen.

What survived the week most strongly was the idea of a representation becoming active. Not just “AI knows things about you”, but something begins doing things you normally need to be there to do: speaking, explaining, making, remembering, correcting, deciding. I still think that is more interesting than whether the system literally becomes human.

I am also not sure I even want the project to answer what remains “uniquely human” anymore. Maybe that question is too grand and maybe it makes it sound like I am looking for one final ingredient that proves people special. I think I am more interested in what happens when something is close enough that other people or even the participant stop caring about the difference.

One sentence I would still stand on from that week: A machine does not have to become you for its version of you to start having power.
